#1999. YM go Global as new stadium sponsor is named

The new name will replace The Herbert Direct Stadium, with new signage recently installed at the ground.

Horsham YM have thanked Herbert Direct for their valued support and sponsorship, saying they are grateful for the company’s backing and the part they have played in supporting football in Horsham.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Herbert Direct are a family-run business based in Broadbridge Heath, supplying kitchen and furniture components to customers across the UK. Founded by John and Sharon Herbert in 2003, the company has strong local roots.

The club now welcome HSM Global as the new stadium naming sponsor. Founded in 2008, HSM Global are a specialist logistics and supply chain business with operations in Horsham and South Wales. Their services span aerospace logistics, global logistics and fulfilment, supporting customers across the UK and internationally.

Geoff Foreman, chairman of Horsham YM Football Club, said: “First and foremost, we want to say a heartfelt thank-you to everyone at Herbert Direct. Their support has been greatly appreciated, and we are proud to have carried their name at our ground.’

"We are also delighted to welcome HSM Global as our new stadium sponsor. It is fantastic to build relationships with businesses that has a presence here in Horsham, and we look forward to welcoming the HSM Global team to the club.”

Hanson Masih, Managing Director of HSM Global, said: "We are delighted to be supporting Horsham YM and to become the club’s stadium naming sponsor.’

"Horsham is an important part of our business’s story, and this partnership is an opportunity to give something back locally. We look forward to getting to know the players, volunteers, and supporters, and to building a positive relationship with the club.”

On the pitch, YM continue to struggle. They lost 3-0 at AFC Varndeanians in the SCFL Premier last Saturday and had Conner Collcutt sent off.

YM will hope for better in Saturday’s derby at home to Billingshurst.

#1998. Aberdeen hero's sobering verdict on lost identity, Cormack's big headache and Pittodrie's revolving door

Alex McLeish reckons Aberdeen chairman Dave Cormack will be “agonising” over their current predicament, suggesting he faces a huge challenge to restore the club's standing as a powerhouse of Scottish football amid another deeply disappointing campaign.

The Dons' ongoing struggles resulted in manager Stephen Robinson being sacked on Monday, with the Northern Irishman relieved of his duties after eight months in charge as results continued to fall short of expectations.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Aberdeen’s hierarchy scheduled a hastily-arranged meeting to discuss the 51-year-old’s future in the wake of a 4-0 defeat at home to Hibs on Saturday, which left the Pittodrie side languishing in 11th place in the Scottish Premiership table.

With concerns surrounding the direction of the club, McLeish feels the problems confronting Aberdeen extend beyond the man in the dugout as he pointed towards poor recruitment, player confidence and a lack of collective identity as key issues which have all resulted in Robinson’s downfall.

Having witnessed the commitment Cormack has shown to the club, McLeish believes he will be feeling the weight of responsibility more than most after standing by his beloved team through some particularly difficult periods.

“Dave is a close friend and I know he's done everything in his power to try and get the Dons to a level,” he said. “We've seen a Scottish Cup final victory a couple of seasons ago. But the league positions are not what Aberdeen fans expect.

‘He will be agonising. You know what it’s like if you get something wrong, you can't sleep at night, can you? Dave will have been through all that kind of rigmarole as well. There'll be a big burden on him right now.

“But he's been stoic and he's stood by the club. He has to be given massive credit for that. It's just about getting Aberdeen to cement their name back at the higher echelons of Scottish football.”

That 2025 Scottish Cup triumph under Jimmy Thelin had offered hope that Aberdeen could use it as a springboard towards challenging more consistently at the top end of the league. Instead, the club have found themselves repeatedly struggling to establish the momentum required to compete with the likes of Celtic, Rangers and Hearts.

The frustration for McLeish is that the rebuilding process has yet to deliver the sustained progress supporters have been demanding.

“I've not got a solution unfortunately, but it's obviously down to acquiring players of a certain level,” he declared. “So, do they have to look at their recruitment? Is it just players that have lost their identity, lost their confidence? These are two massive factors in the world of football.”

The inevitable consequence of a prolonged run of poor results is that the manager becomes the most vulnerable figure. Robinson found himself in precisely that situation, with McLeish claiming that the pressure may have become impossible to withstand as results showed no signs of improving.

He has sympathy for Robinson, particularly given the difficulties of trying to turn around a struggling team when the responsibility for recruitment and squad construction is shared across the club.

“Is it down to recruitment? Are the players not good enough? The manager will always get the worse side of it, because they can't sack 20 players. It's sad to see. I like Stevie, I met him a few times down south and I thought he'd be good for Aberdeen. But, like everybody else, it's trying to get a team to function together.

”To have forwards that you know can score, to have midfielders that can show a bit of quality, eating a man, one-twos, being accurate with your passing. Every bit of quality factor comes into it. I'm just hoping Stevie can get a couple of good results, but it may even be too late, I don't know.”

The wider concern is Aberdeen's inability to re-establish themselves as a club opponents genuinely fear. McLeish believes fans have been waiting several years for a sustained return to prominence, with occasional moments of encouragement failing to translate into lasting progress.

“We've been waiting on it for four or five years. There's been some signs,” he reflected. “There's been obviously winning the cup that year. You think that's a wee springboard for the coming season and then it's all kind of middle of the league, lower end of the league. What is the solution? It's definitely always down to what kind of players you've got.”

#1997. Former Leeds, Sunderland and Crystal Palace striker and ex-Bristol City midfielder join Crawley Town

Both join on short-term deals ending in early January.

Bringing a wealth of experience from the very highest levels of English football, Wickham arrives with an outstanding footballing pedigree, having represented some of the country's most established clubs, including Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Ipswich Town, Sheffield Wednesday, Leeds United, Cardiff City and Charlton Athletic.

The 33-year-old began his professional career at Ipswich, making his first-team debut at just 16 years old and becoming the club's youngest-ever player at the time. His impressive performances quickly attracted attention from Premier League clubs, eventually earning him a move to Sunderland in 2011.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

During his time at Sunderland, Wickham established himself in the Premier League and played a crucial role in the Black Cats' remarkable survival during the 2013-14 campaign. His goals against Manchester City, Chelsea and Cardiff helped secure vital points, earning him the prestigious Premier League Player of the Month award in April 2014.

Throughout his career, the powerful forward has also enjoyed spells with Sheffield Wednesday, Leeds, Preston North End, MK Dons, Forest Green Rovers, Cardiff and Charlton, gaining extensive experience across the Premier League and English Football League.

Benarous arrives with experience in the EFL Championship and League One, having previously represented Bristol City and Plymouth Argyle, as well as earning international recognition with England at Under-17 level.

Born in Bristol, the 23-year-old joined his boyhood club Bristol City at just six years old, progressing through the club's academy ranks before signing his first professional contract in February 2021, aged 17.

A highly regarded prospect throughout his development, Benarous impressed for City's youth and under-23 sides, including a standout performance in which he scored a hat-trick against Watford under-23s. His performances earned him a place in the first-team picture, making his senior debut in October 2021 during a 2-1 Championship victory over Barnsley at Ashton Gate.

After leaving Bristol City in the summer of 2025, the midfielder joined Plymouth Argyle, adding further senior experience in League One and domestic cup competitions to his footballing CV.

Deals for Wickham and Benarous are both subject to the usual EFL and FA Approvals.

#1996. Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG

Unai Emery’s Aston Villa 2.0 remain under construction but from the wreckage of a difficult summer there has emerged a potential star for the future.

Emery may have now suffered four successive defeats in the Super Cup, yet the big positive from a balmy night in Salzburg was the performance of teenage forward Brian Madjo. Aged 17 years and 212 days, Madjo became the youngest player to start and score in this continental showpiece, just over a week after he was given permission to play for his club.

Signed from Metz for £10m in January, Madjo had been prevented from playing because of Fifa’s rules on the international transfer of minors. Villa’s appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to have him registered was upheld on August 4 and what a prospect he appears.

Born in Enfield but raised in Luxembourg, there has been a huge buzz around him since his arrival in the new year.

Paris St-Germain have produced an abundance of talented teenagers over the years and Madjo did not look out of place here.Désiré Doué’s second-half strike secured PSG the Super Cup – contested by the winners of the Champions League and Europa League – for the second successive year, but Emery will have seen enough to give him renewed confidence.

Desire Doue puts PSG 2-1 ahead despite originally being flagged offside 🫣📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/vnMIZCWJaj

His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Hemmings, 19, has emerged from the academy and already made a real impression on his manager. Despite the high regard for those youngsters, this always appeared likely to be a tough proposition against a full-strength PSG team. Indeed, before this game in Salzburg only 39 per cent of Europa League winners have beaten their Champions League rivals in this fixture.

The French champions did start slowly, but had been cranking up the pressure before taking a 20th minute lead with a spectacular strike from their Georgian superstar.

Doué forced a save from Marco Bizot and, after Villa failed to clear, the loose ball landed in the path of Kvaratskhelia, who cut inside on the left to his right foot before smashing a shot into the roof of the net.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia puts PSG 1-0 ahead vs Aston Villa 🔥📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BIf8njpaSx

It was a strike of sheer power and accuracy, catching Bizot by surprise. PSG briefly appeared in control, but Villa responded superbly. In 17 minutes they created six goal-scoring chances before the outstanding Madjo finally made one of them count.

Before his goal, he had narrowly missed the target twice with a pair of headers from John McGinn’s crosses. Villa also had another opportunity 10 minutes before half-time, when Pacho’s mistake allowed Hemmings to run from the centre circle unopposed. As he entered the penalty area, the PSG defenders had raced back to recover and a promising moment ended with Madjo curling a shot wide.

Brian Madjo with a big chance to put Aston Villa level 😮📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pqsC5Hor15

PSG goalkeeper Matvey Safonov then produced his first save just before the break, turning away Boubacar Kamara’s close-range header. Villa did carve out another golden chance when Madjo’s strength took hm past Pacho, but he hit the outside of the post. Madjo’s moment did come, though, as he once again bullied Pacho to divert a McGinn cross into the roof of the net.

Brian Madjo at 17-years-old scores in the UEFA Super Cup Final 🤯📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PccX7FxjAr

Villa were buoyant, but it was PSG who scored the crucial second goal after Doué was awarded the goal following a VAR review. Doué was sent clear down the right by substitute Ousmane Dembélé and confidently beat Bizot, with reviews concluding that he had been played onside by Matty Cash.

The game was refereed by Omar Artan, the Somali referee who was supposed to officiate at the World Cup but was denied entry to the United States.

It became rather fractious as time began to tick away, with McGinn booked after complaining over the placement of a free-kick. Madjo was replaced by Tammy Abraham with 17 minutes left and this will be an evening he will never forget.

Dembele feeds a pass into the Villa box looking to pick out the run of Hakimi but there is slightly too much on it and Bizot is out to gather.

Aston Villa are running out of time to find a late equaliser.

Maatsen brings Dembele down not far outside the Aston Villa box but play goes on as the latter gets up and shoots, with his effort saved by Bizot.

Mayulu is coming on for Doue, whose goal may well have won back-to-back Super Cups for PSG.

PSG are making a double substitution as Ruiz and L Hernandez come on. Neves and Mendes, who had been struggling with cramp, go off.

Aston Villa are going to make a triple change as Abraham, Alysson and Bogarde come on. 17-year-old Madjo is one of those to be replaced as is McGinn, who has been booked as he goes off. The Aston Villa captain is distinctly unimpressed with the officials.

The space opens up for Mendes to take on the shot from range and he obliges, forcing Bizot into a decent save. Kvaratskhelia is unable to make contact with the follow-up. Mendes seems to be struggling with some cramp.

We are nearly 70 minutes into the game but Unai Emery has still not turned to his bench yet.

Aston Villa have an immediate chance to equalise through Hemmings but the 19-year-old’s effort from inside the box is straight at Safonov. That was a big chance for Hemmings.

Down the other end, Gomes is booked for a challenge from behind on Doue.

The VAR has checked it and there was no offside so the original decision is overturned and the goal is given. Doue is played in behind by Dembele down the right channel and is played onside by Cash on the far side. Doue takes it into the Villa penalty area and gets it onto his left foot. Doue has the ball in the Aston Villa net but the offside flag has gone up. However, has Cash played Doue onside?

Mendes is a touch fortunate not to be penalised for a foul on McGinn as the Aston Villa captain spun the Portuguese defender on halfway. The referee must have thought both players had a hold of each other but I would lean towards Mendes probably fouling McGinn.

Other than 10/15 minutes in and around Kvaratskhelia’s goal, Aston Villa have put in a good performance and have created more chances than PSG. If anything, it will be Villa who will be disappointed that they have not scored more than once.

Just inside the PSG penalty area, McGinn cuts onto his left to get his shot away and his deflected effort is saved by Safonov diving to his right.

One of Aston Villa’s coaches has been booked for some protestations after Torres is penalised for a foul on Doue. Torres is also booked for that challenge.

Two of Aston Villa’s best players tonight thus far have been teenagers; 19-year-old Hemmings and 17-year-old Madjo. Aston Villa have seen some key, senior players depart this summer but will take joy from the performances of this pair.

Luis Enrique has decided he needed to make a change at the break as Dembele replaces Akliouche, who was quiet on his official debut for PSG after his move from Monaco.

Incredible to think he is only 17 years and 212 days old. He’s been all over PSG centre-back Willian Pacho and thoroughly deserves his goal.

The teenager could even have had a hat-trick. What a second-half this could be.

Madjo has managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s Georgian magician Kvicha Kvaratskhelia, which is quite some achievement.

After one added minute, the first half is brought to an end and we are all square at 1-1 in Salzburg. Kvaratskhelia had put PSG in front but Madjo’s goal on the stroke of half-time has Aston Villa level at the break.

On the stroke of half-time, the 17-year-old levels for Aston Villa and finally takes his fourth big chance of the night. It is perhaps the hardest chance he has had as McGinn’s cross comes all the way to the back post. Madjo is being held by Pacho but somehow gets his foot to it and his shot goes into the roof of the net. What a moment for the 17-year-old!

Madjo has his third massive chance of this first half and this shot comes off the post. Buendia feeds a pass forward into the path of Madjo, who appeared to be blocked by Pacho but he outmuscles him. Madjo then fires towards goal but it strikes the outside of the post. In a parallel universe, Madjo could have ahd a first-half hat-trick.

Aston Villa have had a few great chances in this first half and there is another. A free-kick into the PSG penalty area causes issues for the French side and Kamara’s header towards goal is saved by Safonov.

Aston Villa have just settled things down. Either side of Kvaratskhelia’s goal, they were on the ropes but have calmed things down.

Hemmings is played in and he could potentially have gone down twice under challenges from Hakimi and then Mendes. The ball then falls to 17-year-old Madjo on the left side of the box. He opens up his body and tries to curl into the far corner but his effort goes wide.

Referees are now hot on players taking too long over throw-ins, with Mendes falling foul of that. That is one of the fairly new rules that will be good for the game.

A huge chance for 17-year-old Madjo to equalise. McGinn picks out the young striker with a sublime cross from the right. Madjo is just eight yards out and has a free header but it goes just wide of the far post. Aston Villa should be level.

After Aston Villa had made a solid start to this game, it is all PSG right now and Villa are on the ropes at the moment. PSG work it beautifully down their left after a sublime one-two between Mendes and Kvaratskhelia. Mendes drives down the left wing and has a cross into the box first-time which he declines. The Portuguese defender then has four different teammates that he could pick out in the penalty area but his cross misses all four.

PSG want a penalty. Kvaratskhelia shows great feet out on the left to drive into the Aston Villa penalty area. Gomes is on his back and Kvaratskhelia goes down. It did look like he was always looking to go down and it would have been very soft.

A few minutes after I said that Aston Villa had done a decent job of keeping PSG at bay, Luis Enrique’s side take the lead. Bizot had just made a great reflex save to deny Doue but he is unable to stop Kvaratskhelia’s effort. The Georgian cuts inside onto his right just inside the Aston Villa penalty area and gets his shot away quickly after quick feet. There is great venom on the shot and it beats Bizot, who thought Kvaratskhelia was going to go for the far corner but instead hit it at the near post. Could Bizot have saved that? Perhaps but Kvaratskhelia did belt that shot.

As you would expect, PSG are dominating possession but thus far have been unable to create any genuine chances, much to Aston Villa’s credit. But, with the players PSG have at their disposal, they can cause chaos in a moment.

Tensions just start to simmer. McGinn gives a foul away on Mendes, who then attempts to take the free-kick a good few yards further forward from where it was. McGinn repeatedly tries to stop Mendes from taking it further forward before the referee steps in to end the dispute.

Moments later, Kamara decides to shoot from range and his low, driving effort goes wide of Safonov’s right post. With Onana injured long-term and Tielemans now at Manchester United, Kamara’s importance to Aston Villa is even higher.

In last year’s Super Cup, PSG were stunned in the first hour against Tottenham as went 2-0 down before coming back to win on penalties. PSG have played fewer friendlies than Aston Villa up until this point so there may be a little more rustiness in Luis Enrique’s side than Unai Emery’s.

This is going to be a very tall order for Aston Villa, who look very different tonight to how they ended last season, up against a team of PSG’s calibre. Not only have Villa sold some key players like Rogers and Tielemans but the likes of Konsa and Watkins are yet to return after the World Cup.

McGinn is afforded too much space and time to cut onto his left foot out on the right and whip a dangerous cross towards the far post. Pacho is on hand to head away with a great defensive header.

What will we learn from the “new Aston Villa” tonight? After the sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, this is a Villa team in transition.

Unai Emery virtually admitted last night it could be another slow start to the season, like last year. Villa face a full-strength PSG team hoping to win the Super Cup for the second time in a row.

I don’t think we can take much from this result tonight, whatever it is. Villa cannot be properly judged until the window closes. Don’t bother telling that to Unai Emery, though. He is ready to continue defying the doubters.

The Champions League and Europa League winners fight it out in the Uefa Super Cup in Salzburg as PSG take on Aston Villa. PSG took on English opposition in the Super Cup a year ago, when they played Tottenham. PSG fell 2-0 down in that game in Udine but scored two late goals to take it to penalties, where they won 4-3. These sides met in the Champions League knockout stages two seasons ago; PSG did progress from the quarter-final encounter as they went on to win the competition but not without a scare as Aston Villa did win at Villa Park and PSG only progressed 5-4 on aggregate. The two clubs have been involved in a transfer this week, with left-back Lucas Digne re-joining PSG from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa have played in the Super Cup once before back in 1982 when they took in Barcelona. They lost the first leg 1-0 over at Camp Nou but fought back to win the second leg 3-0 at Villa Park to claim the trophy. Aston Villa were last in action out in the Far East last Friday, falling to a 2-1 defeat to Bayern Munich in Hong Kong. It has been a big summer of change at the club, with key starters like Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans departing and the likes of Alejandro Garnacho and Joao Gomes arriving.

“I feel like the club is in a new era, with this possibility to fight for trophies,” Unai Emery told Uefa. “We are trying to be successful through, firstly, [building] a winning team, and then aiming for the positive consequences after it; winning trophies. To play the UEFA Super Cup is another opportunity to be there, the opportunity to win a trophy, to play against Paris Saint-Germain; the [best] team in the world now and another team we can compare [ourselves] with.”

Emery has confirmed that Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins and Emiliano Martinez will not be involved as they are still on their breaks following the World Cup.

PSG have now won back-to-back Champions Leagues, beating Arsenal in the final last season. They have only played a couple of friendlies in pre-season, losing 3-0 to Mallorca before drawing 1-1 against Manchester United. Luis Enrique’s side will take on Lens in the Trophée des Champions on Sunday before kicking off the defence of their Ligue 1 title at home to Rennes.

“I focus on renewing that desire to win again,” Enrique told Uefa. “It is difficult to keep winning. Right now, we have a unique challenge; something that is practically unprecedented in the history of European football, which is to draw level with Real Madrid if we can win a third consecutive Champions League. No-one in history has won three in a row, only Real Madrid. We can equal them. But I do not think there is any team in Europe more motivated than us.

“No-one rules out PSG any more. Two years ago, it was impossible to put us among the favourites; not impossible, but we were not one of the favourites. Now, no one would say that Paris Saint-Germain are not the favourites. That is something we have earned, but if we are going to maintain that position, we have to work even harder.”

PSG have added Monaco winger Maghnes Akliouche and Digne to their ranks this summer. They are also pushing to sign Ferran Torres from Barcelona and Mika Godts from Ajax. Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye have both been linked with moves to Liverpool but have been included in their squad for tonight’s game, as have Akliouche and Digne.

#1995. How forgotten Celtic and PSG star nearly joined Rangers as lid lifted on 'advanced negotiatons'

Former Celtic midfielder Youssouf Mulumbu has revealed how he came very close to joining Rangers after holding “advanced negotiations” with the Ibrox club.

Mulumbu joined Celtic from Kilmarnock in 2018 and spent a year at the club, making a handful of appearances. However, the DR Congo internationalist could easily have been representing the other side of the Old Firm.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

“Football is crazy,” said Mulumbu. “I'll tell you the story of how I signed for Celtic - I was actually in advanced negotiations with Rangers.

“We were finalising the contract when negotiations suddenly stalled out of nowhere. I returned to France, and out of the blue, Brendan Rodgers called me personally. He spoke to me at length about the club and how he planned to integrate me.

“Looking back, I should have shown more patience. Instead of asking to go out on loan the moment I wasn't starting, I should have stayed, fought for my place in training, and waited for my opportunity. With hindsight, had I stayed put, I would have played far more games for Celtic.

“Moving to Celtic was a dream because I had always wanted to play for an elite club competing for silverware. The dynamic was very different from Kilmarnock, though. Celtic already had established midfield leaders, Scott Brown, Callum McGregor, and Nir Bitton.

“Forcing my way into that starting lineup was difficult. We had dropped into the Europa League after missing out on Champions League qualification, but Brendan Rodgers already had a settled tactical structure and preferred starting eleven.

“It was tough to break through, but playing at Celtic Park in front of those passionate fans was a special experience. In hindsight, I feel I could and should have done more to secure regular minutes.”

Former PSG youth Mulumbu, who also had spells at Norwich City and West Brom, had a far more fruitful time at Kilmarnock under Steve Clarke, who he worked with at the Baggies.

“Kilmarnock was incredible, you know,” the 39-year-old continued. I arrived there after a bad spell at Norwich where I had lost the passion for football. But I spoke with Steve Clarke at the time, and he told me to come and enjoy my football.

“Obviously, it's not the same wages and it's not the same facilities, but I was surprised because when I arrived there, I really enjoyed training every day and playing against good sides like Celtic, Rangers, and Aberdeen. And I discovered a country as well, you know. Different mentality, different culture. It was very, very good.

“I had played five games when I arrived, and after that, I was supposed to be transferred to Bordeaux in France. I remember I spoke with Steve Clarke and I spoke with the president at the time, and they were really sad because I was doing well. And the transfer failed.”

Adding in an interview with Paris Match Casino, Mulumbu went on: “As the transfer failed on the Friday, we then played on Sunday against Celtic and I scored! All right, yeah, we won 1–0, for the story! And no, that was very, very nice mentally, you know, because after what happened at Norwich, to come back as a football player and to play for a team that loves you, where you can feel the love of the supporters and of your teammates, that was great.”

#1994. Three Bridges show fighting spirit to earn point against Brentwood Town

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Three Bridges produced a spirited performance on Saturday at Jubilee Field, earning a 1-1 draw against Brentwood Town after an evenly contested encounter. Bridges were desperate to get points on the board, but perhaps even more importantly, to rediscover the battling spirit that had been missing during last week's disappointing performance away at Maldon & Tiptree. Jamie Crellin's men responded positively, showing plenty of fight and determination throughout.

After an even opening, the hosts took the lead in the 12th minute through October's Club Player of the Month, Ade Adeyinka. David Przybylo played Ade through the middle and, from around 20 yards out, he unleashed an unstoppable strike into the net to give Bridges an early advantage.

The remainder of the first half was evenly matched, with Roberts producing several good saves in the Bridges goal. At the other end, the energetic Villavicencio continued to cause problems for the visitors, particularly with a dangerous cross towards Reece Hallard, whose header from six yards narrowly missed the target. Bridges went into the interval holding a deserved 1-0 lead.

It could have been 2-0 just moments into the second half as, straight from the restart, Bridges put together an excellent move down the right. Velvick released Przybylo through on goal, but under pressure from the goalkeeper, his effort narrowly drifted wide.

Brentwood Town began to pile on the pressure at the other end and found their reward in the 58th minute. Following a free-kick from Reid, Gibbs slotted his effort into the bottom corner to restore parity.

Just a couple of minutes later, Przybylo, who had been a constant handful for the visitors, worked his way past his marker and had another opportunity to restore Bridges' advantage, but his effort narrowly missed the far post.

With Bridges short of options on the bench and several players playing through injuries, maintaining the intensity became increasingly difficult. Brentwood Town took control during the final 20 minutes, but Roberts came to the rescue with two superb saves to deny Cerulli and Sears, while the Bridges players continued to put their bodies on the line to protect their point.

There was late drama in the 94th minute when Reece Hallard chased a ball through on the counter-attack, only for Cripps to handle it as the last man. The Brentwood defender was shown a straight red card, leaving the visitors down to ten men. However, it came too late to have any impact on the outcome, as the match finished 1-1.

The point represents a much-needed response from Bridges, who will now face a demanding run of three consecutive away fixtures in seven days. First up is a trip to Cray Wanderers on Tuesday 10 November (19:45), followed by a visit to Welling United on Saturday 14 November (15:00), before another Tuesday evening journey to Dartford on 17 November (19:45).

Three Bridges Line-up: Roberts, Irving, Neathey (C), Malone, J. Hallard, Villavicencio (Chambers 87), Adeyinka, Przybylo (Richards 77), Velvick, R. Hallard, Bennett.

Player of the Match – Sam Roberts: An impressive display from Roberts in goal, producing several outstanding saves to keep Bridges in the contest. The young goalkeeper also impressed with his distribution, setting his side on the attack with some excellent kicking. A thoroughly deserved Player of the Match award.

#1991. Scott McTominay 'had shock on heart' before Scotland World Cup game as ex-Man Utd star opens up on summer

Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay has revealed that he needed to have his heart “shocked” two days before the nation’s World Cup opener against Haiti.

McTominay explained that he was taken to hospital 48 hours before the match on June 14 and was “put to sleep”. At the time, his absence from training was put down to a sickness bug, but the 29-year-old has spoken for the first time on what he went through during the summer.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

McTominay played the full 90 minutes in the 1-0 win over the Haitians and started the next two games against Morocco and Brazil, which Scotland lost to exit the tournament at the group stage.

McTominay then went on holiday before returning to his club side Napoli, who announced on September 1 that the former Man Utd player was to have a procedure to correct a "mild benign arrhythmia". He missed the last international window under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli, but is now back in the camp for matches against North Macedonia and Switzerland in the coming days.

“I’m good,” said McTominay in his broadcast press conference on Tuesday. “I’m feeling much, much better than I was. I feel like it was something that needed to be done. In your career you have moments like that where things like that can take you by surprise. It looks a lot worse in the media for family and friends - they see news relating to a heart issue - but it’s a relatively straightforward procedure that went really well. I’m really happy to be back and playing football again. That’s the most important thing.

“I feel like it was explained to me really, really well by the doctors at Napoli and my cardiologist in Manchester alongside the doctor in Scotland when we were away at the World Cup. He explained that if this was the case, this is how it would look. Credit to all the staff members, they made me so relaxed about the situation.”

Explaining how the World Cup unfolded, McTominay continued: “The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game. You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking ‘how has this happened to me’. But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football. Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say ‘well, it’s part of the process.’

“Obviously the way the World Cup went, there were at least two, three weeks of me sitting there disappointed, not quite there mentally. I needed time to settle down and have a break.

“I was 100 per cent [fitness wise], but whenever you are sat in a hospital bed two days before the World Cup, about to get put to sleep, it’s not ideal, is it? So whenever things like that happen ... it is what it is, there’s nothing you can do about it. After the World Cup, I reflected on it and I was extremely disappointed. Probably the most disappointed I’ve ever been in my career.

“After the World Cup, my summer holidays weren’t heavily centred around thinking about the World Cup, but it plays a part. Whenever you are disappointed or angry about something, you go away on your holidays and it’s just not the same. You are sat there thinking ‘we could have done more’ but that three-week break I had with my operation done me the world of good.

“I’m always one to be glass half-full but after the World Cup I was like ‘this is a tough one to take’. But you have to refresh and you have to come out stronger at the other side.”

#1990. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EST, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.

#1988. Scott McTominay given police escort as drama 36 hours before Scotland World Cup clash laid bare

Scott McTominay has revealed he had to have a police escort to a hospital in Boston to have his heart ‘shocked’ 36 hours before Scotland’s opening World Cup game against Haiti.

At the time, his absence from training and travel arrangements to Boston – he travelled from the team’s base in Charlotte separately from the rest of the team – were attributed to a stomach bug. In fact, it was a heart condition known as atrial fibrillation.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

“You're not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“It's not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before—well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup. But you have to take the cards that you're dealt on the chin. It's part of the game. There's nothing I could do about it.”

Some will question the decision to let him play in not only the match against Haiti, which Scotland won 1-0, but also the two following group games against Morocco and Brazil. The Scots lost both fixtures and exited the World Cup with McTominay perceived to have been under par.

“It was in my hands,” he said. “The medical team reassured me it was safe to play and they said: ‘What do you think?' I said: ‘Let’s go for it’.”

Unbeknown to nearly everyone, and while Scotland fans were drinking bars dry in Boston, McTominay was at the centre of incredible drama.

Manager Steve Clarke told reporters that the midfielder had been laid low by a stomach bug. The reality of the situation - and the fact it was kept secret for so long - is barely believable given the global attention on the tournament and that McTominay is Scotland's star player.

He himself sought to downplay the situation on Tuesday at Hampden as he revealed the true story for the first time. “We got a police escort to go and get the shock then that was it to be honest,” recalled McTominay. “After that, I was back in normal rhythm, which is how a healthy heart should be then I went and played the game two days later.”

He described being put under anaesthetic. “You have to get put to sleep,” he said. “Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and (affects) sleep and stuff like that. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you're dealt, there's nothing you can do about it.”

Although he stressed his family were fully on board with him playing, he wouldn’t have listened had it been otherwise. “All my family and friends had just flown 10 hours for the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“I didn’t sit there thinking I might not play. That would never be the case. I was always going to play in that game. Maybe selfishly, I don’t know but that’s football. Players play with injuries all the time when they’re not quite right and it might be to the detriment of the team. (But) I was fully functional.”

The Napoli midfielder has since undergone an operation after the problem resurfaced following an early season Serie A game against Como. He returned to Manchester, where he had a procedure known as pulsed field ablation.

The player was sidelined for several weeks, missing the first games under new Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli but has returned to the squad for upcoming Nations League games against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

#1986. Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end

Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

It was a shame because in that cameo, Fernandes showed he has returned from the World Cup in excellent shape, the tempo of United’s play immediately lifting when he had the ball. It is wrong to make conclusions in the summer, but you are on safe ground to state he will be integral to their ambitions.

Croke Park is a stadium steeped in history and another chapter was penned here, as the capacity crowd made this the highest attended soccer match in Ireland with 82,000 coming through the gates: it is a magnificent venue, one that would be well capable of hosting a Champions League final.

Michael Carrick hopes in years to come that is the stage where his team will be but, right now, it is a case of learning to walk again before they can run and he more than anyone will know how far off that target is, not that it will stop him trying to get there.

The one thing that is obvious about the way United play under him is the first thought from everyone is to go forward quickly. Yes, this was only a friendly, but the ambition to be on the front foot and cause problems was evident from the start.

The team in red had much the better of the opening exchanges, with Diogo Dalot having the first shot that went over but, unlike on July 25, when Mayo beat Kerry here in Gaelic football’s All Ireland final, which went viral, nobody was cheering the sight of a ball clearing the bar.

It was like a home game for United and the majority got what they wanted in the 15th minute when a slick counter-attack ended with Bryan Mbuemo sliding a pass into Joshua Zikzee, who rifled past James Trafford with a first-time finish.

Devastating counterattack! 💥Manchester United break and Joshua Zirkzee is there to finish it off 🤩 pic.twitter.com/y6QHbZMi7n

Zirkzee is unlikely to be part of Carrick’s squad beyond the transfer window, with interest from clubs in Italy, and it would be disingenuous to suggest his career at Old Trafford has been successful, but his attitude was exemplary and he played as if he was desperate to change his manager’s mind.

There may have been an anticipation that United would stride clear, but this game was also about Leeds, whose summer has been encouraging and whose confidence from staying up last season has evidently enabled them to blossom.

You would be way off the mark if you include them in your conversations about which clubs are going to be relegated next May, and the sense they showed to stay with Daniel Farke has paid off. They have bought some good players, not least goalkeeper James Trafford and Harry Wilson.

Top stop from James Trafford! 🚫The Leeds United keeper has been busy in the first half... pic.twitter.com/VKmxNVKBsA

Trafford has done the right thing getting away from Manchester City and you could argue that he is already reaping the benefit of playing for a manager who wants him, as he made a fabulous save in the 23rd minute to thwart Mbuemo. It was all part of performance that led to him being named player of the match.

He was involved in the move that brought the Leeds equaliser, too, as his long clearance caused uncertainty and led to Tyler Fletcher being pickpocketed by Dan James and he nudged a pass into Brenden Aaronson, who kept his cool and danced into the area, ignoring Senne Lammens, to finish.

Leeds hit back with their first shot on target! 💥Brenden Aaronson with a cool finish 🥶 pic.twitter.com/5WsSZY41j6

It was an entertaining affair, mercifully lacking the bile that would usually bubble away when it is staged in England, and the longer the game advanced, the better Leeds looked. They finished the opening period strongly and came back after the restart, with 10 changes, in the same fettle.

Farke, whose team had shown their ability to score heavily when they pummelled Liverpool 4-2 in Chicago 10 days ago, would have taken plenty of encouragement, but the perfectionist in him would have cursed the opportunities that were squandered early in the second period.

The misses proved costly as the game meandered and the shoot-out went United’s way, after Wilson and James Justin failed from 12 yards, with Noussair Mazraoui thumping in the decisive kick. It really is never dull.

Decent enough watch for roughly half the game, settled on a shoot-out in which Alex Cairns got nowhere near any of Manchester United’s penalties. Doubt he will lose much sleep over it. Bruno Fernandes grinned broadly when he missed.

Bottom left. Manchester United win the Boyle Sports Cup.

Smacks it even higher into the top right.

And I think Amapdu’s signal means Leeds will go first.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the pre-season friendly between Manchester United and Leeds United at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin. Last year Leeds played Milan in the Irish capital and drew a crowd of 52,000 but at the GAA citadel, as I think I’m contractually obliged to call it, there will be 83,000 present, a testament to the Premier League’s reach and these two clubs’ popularity in Ireland founded on the exploits of Billy Whelan, Noel Cantwell, Johnny Giles, Roy Keane, Gary Kelly et al. It’s the first club match ever held at the stadium.

It’s a fixture that always stirs the blood and whenever it comes around you can guarantee that there will be reams of stuff about the War of the Roses, clash in styles, Busby and Revie, Bobby and Jack, large swathes of which this author has been guilty of producing. I’ll spare you all that today because while it’s relevant to fans of both clubs, they know it backwards. And it’s a match that has come around a wee bit too frequently in pre-season recently, first in Perth, Western Australia, in 2019 when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s side beat Marcelo Bielsa’s 4-0, then in 2023 in Oslo when Erik ten Haag’s second or third string defeated Daniel Farke’s threadbare, just relegated squad 2-0 and last year in Stockholm, which ended in a 0-0 draw between two scratch sides.

This one comes round later in the pre-season schedule than those three so we can expect to see stronger XIs, at least for part of the game. Leeds’ pre-season has gone well: after a 3-2 defeat by Wrexham in Tampa, they have beaten Sunderland in New Jersey, Liverpool in Chicago and RB Leipzig at Elland Road. Manchester United also lost to Wrexham (in Helsinki) then beat Rosenborg in Trondheim, Atlético in Stockholm and drew one apiece with the European champions, PSG, in Gothenburg last time out.

While Leeds will have new signing James Trafford available and Noah Okafor, who scored twice in Leeds’ first league victory at Old Trafford for 45 years last April, in the squad for the first time after the World Cup, Manchester United have Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford back in training since the start of the week but it seems too soon for them to start but Youri Tielemans is pushing to make his first start.

#1984. Scott McTominay: I didn't know what people were saying about me and the World Cup

Picture the scene. Scotland fans are drinking Boston’s bars dry. Meanwhile, unbeknown to them, their star player, their main hope, was getting a police escort to a hospital in the city to have his heartbeat jolted back into a normal pattern. Scotland tend to make a drama out of World Cups, but this is something else.

It is almost a year to the day since Scott McTominay wowed the world with an overhead kick to set Scotland on the way to qualifying for the tournament for the first time in 28 years against Denmark. This might have been expected to be a main topic of conversation as the player sat down for an all-too rare interview at Hampden on Tuesday.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In the end, however, this scintillating piece of skill, immortalised on a tenement gable end near Hampden, proved barely an afterthought. McTominay consents to interviews only very infrequently, certainly in Scotland. When he does do them, they seem like events.

This is especially the case when he is recalling being blue lighted through the streets of Boston a couple of evenings before Scotland were due to make their long-awaited return to the World Cup against Haiti.

It is scarcely believable that having had his heart effectively reset, he was lining up against the Caribbean nation in a pulsating World Cup encounter a mere 36 hours later. He very nearly even scored.

The Napoli midfielder watched a shot crash off the post in the first half shortly before John McGinn scored with a deflected effort that proved the winner. Although he was so close to getting on the scoresheet, the general perception was that McTominay struggled to shake off the effects of the “stomach bug” that had been communicated as the reason for his absence from training two days beforehand.

The midfielder was considered never to have reached the heights expected of him during Scotland’s tournament, which lasted another two games. It must have been excruciatingly irritating for him to read such verdicts and be unable to respond.

He was even rated in some quarters as among the tournament’s biggest flops. The Scotland staff couldn’t say anything, nor could he. He claims he was oblivious to the criticism.

“I didn’t know that’s what people were saying,” he said. “Although I probably had an idea. I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it.

“You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be. For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.”

There might be a lot of people eating humble pie having been informed of the true nature of McTominay’s health problem. It’s no one’s fault. You can’t refer to such a serious mitigating factor if it’s being – understandably – kept hidden. McTominay explained to rapt reporters the details behind his condition, which is known as atrial fibrillation. In other words, an unsteady heartbeat. He even provided some sound effects. Who says McTominay is an unwilling interviewee?

“Atrial fibrillation is a fairly normal routine thing for people in general,” he said. “They might not know that they have it. But when you're an elite athlete in general across the board, across football, across sports in general, you know if you've got something that's different.

“Whenever you're running and you check your pulse and it's got a slight irregular beat there, it feels like your heart's coming out of your chest.

“Not obviously as bad as that but that's the sensation that you have. It's pumping, but not a regular heartbeat like bum, bum, bum, bum. Mine's going bum, bu-bu-bum, bum, bu-bu-bum. So you know the difference.”

You also know that it’s not something you would wish to develop on the eve of the World Cup that is being played in intense temperatures.

“The heat was tough, that was probably the hardest part,” he reflected. “But I’ve worked for 20 years as a young footballer and as a professional to get to that point, to try and play well at a World Cup.” Nothing, he stressed, was going to stop him, not even lying on a hospital bed under anaesthetic two evenings before the first game while an electrode is placed on his chest.

He has since been back in hospital for a more involved procedure. Napoli released a statement in September to say the minimally invasive operation known as cardiac ablation surgery had been “a complete success” although McTominay missed several matches, including the first four Nations League fixtures under new manager Sebastien Pocognoli.

“I went into that surgery with no doubt in my mind that I’d be back,” he said. “I lost a little bit of muscle when I came out, three or four kilos which wasn’t ideal. I had to put that back on pretty sharpish.

“The first picture of me when I came back, I looked quite gaunt. So I had to get that muscle back so I could get back my powerful running and what I normally do on a football pitch.

“It was a good reset period for me,” he added. “No matter how long it took - even if it took until I was 40! - I was coming back to try and do my best. I’ve had a good time to reflect on the World Cup and think about things leading up to it.

“When I had the operation I had three weeks at home. I didn’t watch as much football as I normally do. I (normally) watch every game of football, every night. It’s relentless with me.

“Games in the Champions League, Europa League, Scottish football, the Premier League, Serie A - I watch a lot now compared to when I was younger.

“So I had three weeks of resting my mind more than anything to try and come back in a better state.”

It’s good news for the Tartan Army, who are desperate for McTominay, who turns 30 next month, to rescue Scotland from an unsure start to the Nations League under Pocognoli. The Belgian has stressed he wants to find a way of taking the burden off those such as McTominay. But the player himself doesn’t mind the extra responsibility. Indeed, he relishes it.

“He's mentioned that to me before about maybe taking a little bit (of the burden) and putting it across the whole board, but I don’t see football like that,” he said.

“I don’t go into a game thinking that the people watching really need me to do something here so I try to do different things, you just play the game, don’t you?

“Express yourself and play how you would normally play, and the rest will take care of itself, you don’t need to overthink about pressure.

“I’ve played at Man United, I’ve played at Napoli, I know what pressure is. I’ve played for Scotland in the World Cup, I know what pressure is. It’s not the worst thing in the world that can happen to you. It’s a privilege to have things expected of you.”

Pocognoli told reporters last week that he was looking forward to making a connection with someone generally identified as Scotland’s star player. It seems he is already well on the way to achieving this despite the pair only having met in the flesh for the first time earlier this week.

It was Pocognoli's idea for McTominay to sit down with the media at Hampden on Tuesday, an instruction he obeyed.

“I like his ideas a lot,” said McTominay “Whenever I first had a meeting with him, I liked the way that he wants to play the game.”

At the end of the near 15-minute conversation with McTominay, an annual at best occurrence, there was just about enough time to reference the approaching one-year anniversary of That goal. And mention That 36ft tall mural, which was unveiled earlier this year.

“Unreal,” he said. “I don’t know how I feel. I obviously like it, it’s incredible, but if you were asking me, you don’t want my big ugly face up there!”

#1983. Didier Deschamps 'doesn't want Manchester United job': Blow for Sir Jim Ratcliffe as unemployed former France boss appears hesitant to replace under-fire Michael Carrick

Published: 04:37 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 04:37 EST, 6 November 2026

Manchester United have suffered a road bump in sounding out potential replacements for Michael Carrick – as Didier Deschamps reportedly doesn't want the gig.

Deschamps, who left the France job after 14 years following the World Cup, has told the club he is uninterested according to the Daily Mirror.

Carrick remains in post but his bosses have been privately talking to possible successors for weeks after an abysmal start to the season which has left them 17th in the Premier League.

Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte have all come up on the shortlist, with the international break this month seen as an ideal time for managerial changes across the league.

Deschamps appealed to United because of his immediate availability and lack of a compensation fee, but is in no rush to take a job and snubbed their advance.

After a glittering career as a player, he has won the World Cup managing France, lifted Ligue 1 with Marseille, led Monaco to a Champions League final, and got Juventus promoted back to Serie A after the Calciopoli scandal.

Didier Deschamps has reportedly told Manchester United he is not interested in the job

Michael Carrick remains in post but United have been sounding out potential replacements for weeks

Carrick's prospects of keeping the job had a boost on Tuesday as Matheus Cunha struck two late goals to produce a stunning turnaround win against Roma in the Champions League.

But he only has a clash against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday afternoon before the international break to prove to the hierarchy that he should keep his job.

That comeback against Roma stopped a rot which has been spreading for weeks. United were on the verge of going ten games without a win, a run unprecedented in the club's history.

They have reached a nadir in recent weeks after batterings by Como and Bournemouth – the latter at Old Trafford, no less – while players have been openly mutinous.

Bruno Fernandes publicly criticised Carrick's tactics after the 4-1 defeat at Como, leading to Carrick benching him for the next game against Bournemouth.

And Lisandro Martinez has singled out director of football Jason Wilcox over United's transfer activity, suggesting the squad was left short on quality after the transfer window.

Were Carrick to go, it is unclear who would replace him.

Emery is open to signing a new deal with Aston Villa which would take him to close to a decade at the club, and held a meeting with club chiefs on Wednesday.

Hurzeler does not have a release clause in his Brighton contract and so would require enormous compensation. There is well-placed scepticism as to whether any move would even be remotely possible, regardless of how well liked he is inside Old Trafford.

Nagelsmann and Conte are both out of work and the latter has previously indicated that he would like the challenge of restoring a fallen giant to glory.

Hear hear. They get paid ridiculous sums yet they they did nothing to earn it midweek.

Maybe they were tired, give them more time to rest, it will help them.

Then Amorim needs his captain and 1 – 2 deputies who lead and organize the team on the pitch.

Bad results can happen but it shouldn’t be for lack of effort and hard work. Which is what this was.

#1981. Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

The visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU

Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.

“I think it is a really harsh one. He [the referee] has to be sure at such a critical time of the game. And I do not think he can be sure. I think he has almost had a guess that he is in the box. It is such a big call.”

“We see the ref’s position. The fact the ref makes the decision to give the penalty in my opinion, it is a bigger decision to give it then to not. We have got the luxury of the replays and we are still not sure. His whole body is outside the box.”

“It looks outside the box to me [the penalty incident]. The still picture suggests to me it was outside the box. We can get better and we will have to. We have to be more dominant with the ball at times and be better in attack. We have done a lot of work on that in pre-season. Having been in this league a long time, the power of the dressing room is crucial and any motivation tool you can you use is important. I think we will be fine. You have to enjoy football and love it. I think the boys enjoyed it tonight.”

“Obviously frustrated. The boys did everything to get the three points but it is gutting in the end. I thought I was outside the box when the ball came in and the decision went against us. They are saying it is in the box and it is frustrating. We dug deep and thought we had it. I cannot fault everyone as we all put in a shift, it was just the final details with the penalty decision. We deserved the three points. If we play like that every week, we will go far in the table.”

Raul Jimenez reacts after his late penalty saved a point for Wolves against Blackburn 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/aXvVeWw6fc

“Before the game we were predicting Wolves would be right up there [this season] and we thought it would be a comfortable win. But that was not the case.  Blackburn gave a really good account of themselves and had lots of openings. [Cesar] Peixoto will be breathing a massive sigh of relief with that handball.”

“Wolves got away with one if I am being really honest. In terms of their second-half performance, they did not do anywhere near enough. I thought Blackburn were excellent throughout and deservedly took the lead. It is a huge decision [to give the penalty], but in the end Raul Jimenez steps up to get his side the point. [Cesar Peixoto] will be delighted to get something in the end.”
